choices.term: τῇ τῶν ἱερέων τελειότητι τὸ δοκοῦν ἐλλείπειν, τοῖς τῶν λαῶν ἀναπληρῷτο μέτροις
choices.english: whatever seems lacking in the people’s measure may be made up by the perfection of the priests
rejected: what seems lacking in the perfection of the priests is filled by the measures of the people
choices.why: Cyril's own analogy (the small mixed with the perfect) shows the priests' perfection supplies the people's lack.
ἴδιος here stands for σός, as 1 Corinthians 14:16 has σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ.

choices.english: Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit
rejected: cannot say Amen because they do not understand
choices.why: The lemma is Paul's question (1 Corinthians 14:16), kept as a question.
πρὸς with genitive of the agent: done by us; the goal is the brothers' building up.
ἐν καλῷ, in a good state; paired with firmness of hope.

pass_a_gloss: [Completing the previous section: Spirit in these words he names the grace through the] Spirit, that is, being able to speak in tongues. If then, he says, I pray the prayers in the churches in spirit, that is, having made use of the tongue through the spirit, I shall have the mind fruitless (ἄκαρπος); for in prayers one must be strained toward (συντείνομαι) [God], and seek from God the things that lead toward salvation, not pride oneself (ἐναβρύνομαι) on a tongue and become merely [a man] of speaking in a tongue; since the mind becomes fruitless, carrying away no profit from such ambition (φιλοτιμία). [Lemma] I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind. It is needful for me then, he says, if I should choose to pray in a tongue, that is, to be well thought of (εὐδοκιμέω) in speaking in a tongue, to try earnestly not to have the mind fruitless, nor to become [a man] of speaking with the tongue only, but to rouse up (διεγείρω) the mind in myself; and if I should perhaps sing in a tongue, to sing no less also with the mind, in understanding the force of the psalmody and of the prophecy, and not leave such words unsought (ἀζήτητος). For if I should speak random (εἰκαῖος) sounds, 'I have become sounding brass.' Wherefore it is better to prophesy, or to interpret the divine Scriptures in church, than to love merely to make full use of tongues. What then will be the better? I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind. And by spirit again here he means the gift through the Spirit. And since his aim (σκοπός), through as many and as necessary thoughts as possible, is to show speaking in a tongue unprofitable (ἀνόνητος), when being able to make clear (διατρανόω) to others the things of the prophets does not follow, he brings in still other things through which one might see him speaking clearly. [Lemma] Since if you bless in spirit, the one filling the place of the private man (ἰδιώτης), how will he say the Amen? When, he says, you yourself speak in a tongue, but the one placed in the rank of the layman (λαϊκός), if he should not know your voice, how will he answer (προσυπακούω) the Amen in your own thanksgivings, or prayers? For that it is the custom in churches for the [prayers] of those under hand to end together with (συγκαταλήγω) the prayers of those leading is clear to everyone. For they answer the Amen to their own supplications (ἱκετεία) to God, bringing the end to the voice of the priest, so that what seems to fall short (ἐλλείπω) in the measures of the peoples may be filled up by the perfection of the priests, and God may receive as it were 'the small with the great' as in oneness of spirit. For the peoples under hand, yoking (παραζεύγνυμι) their own [prayers] to the prayers of the priests, have believed they will be acceptable; with this aim God also commanded poor (πενιχρός) sacrifices to be brought to the altar of the whole burnt offerings, so that the small mingled (συμμιγής) with the perfect might become acceptable to God; for we all are one in the Lord. When then, he says, you speak in a tongue (for this is blessing in spirit), the one not knowing what you say, how will he say the Amen at your own thanksgiving? For you yourself will act rightly, at least according to the mind in you, but the other is not built up. And all things must be done by us for building up and for the profit of brothers. [Heading] Tome Five, Discourse Four. [Lemma] And I make known to you, brothers, the gospel which I preached to you. Very much in season and wisely he calls gospel the proclamation about the resurrection of the dead, and in every way of Christ himself; for indeed it is truly the announcement (ἀπαγγελία) of every good to those who have received the faith; and he says that they stand in it and are saved: the standing signifying (κατασημαίνω) the being of believers in firmness (ἑδραιότης) of hope and in a good state of glory; and the being saved, the having been shown up (ἀναφαίνω) [better] even than sin itself [continued in the next section].
pass_b_english: …Spirit, that is, the ability to speak in tongues. So if, he says, I offer the prayers in the churches “in the spirit,” that is, using the tongue given through the Spirit, my mind will be unfruitful (1 Corinthians 14:14). For in prayer one must be intent and seek from God what leads to salvation, not pride oneself on a tongue and give oneself over merely to speaking in a tongue, since then the mind becomes unfruitful and gains no benefit from such display.

“I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). So, he says, if I choose to pray in a tongue, that is, to win esteem by speaking in a tongue, I must take earnest care not to have an unfruitful mind, and not to give myself over only to speaking in the tongue, but to rouse my mind within me. And if I happen to sing in a tongue, I must sing no less with the mind as well, by understanding the meaning of the psalmody and of the prophecy, and not leave such words unexamined (1 Corinthians 14:15). For if I utter empty sounds, “I have become a noisy gong” (1 Corinthians 13:1). So it is better to prophesy, that is, to interpret the divine Scriptures in church, than to be fond of merely using tongues.

What, then, will be the better way? “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Here again by “spirit” he means the gift given through the Spirit. Since his aim, through a great many compelling arguments, is to show that speaking in a tongue is useless unless the ability to make the prophets plain to others goes with it, he adds still further points, in which one can see him saying it clearly.

“Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say the ‘Amen’?” (1 Corinthians 14:16). When you speak in a tongue, he says, how will the one who stands in the rank of the layman, if he does not know your language, answer “Amen” at your thanksgivings, that is, your prayers? For it is plain to everyone that in the churches the custom is for the prayers of those in the leaders’ charge to end together with the prayers of the leaders. They answer “Amen,” closing their own supplications to God at the priest’s words, so that whatever seems lacking in the people’s measure may be made up by the perfection of the priests, and so that God may receive, as it were, “the small together with the great” (Psalm 115:13) as in unity of spirit. For the people in their charge, joining their own prayers to the prayers of the priests, have believed that these will be accepted.

With this aim, too, God commanded that even poor sacrifices be brought to the altar of burnt offerings, so that the small, mixed with the perfect, might become acceptable to God. For we are all one in the Lord. So when you speak in a tongue, he says (for this is what “blessing with the spirit” means), how will the one who does not know what you are saying say the “Amen” at your thanksgiving? You yourself will do well, at least by the understanding that is in you, but the other is not built up (1 Corinthians 14:16–17). Yet everything we do must be done for building up and for the benefit of the brothers (1 Corinthians 14:26).

“Now I make known to you, brothers, the gospel that I preached to you” (1 Corinthians 15:1). Very aptly and wisely he calls the preaching about the resurrection of the dead, and surely also about the resurrection of Christ himself, a gospel, for it truly is the announcement of every good thing to those who have received the faith. And he says that they stand in it and are being saved (1 Corinthians 15:1–2). “To stand” signifies that believers are firm in hope and well established in glory, while “to be saved” signifies that they have even been shown…
